notes.bp: An enhancement model should adapt when the noise at test time differs from training, even without labeled examples from the new environment.
notes.wh: Noise and recording domains shift at deployment, while collecting clean/noisy pairs for every new domain is expensive.
notes.naive: Freeze the enhancement model and hope training-domain noise statistics transfer.
notes.ap: Use a Y-shaped enhancement model with self-supervised reconstruction or masked-spectrogram tasks during test-time adaptation.
notes.mech: The main enhancement task shares representations with an auxiliary task optimized on the current noisy signal, with strategies trading adaptation gain against test-time cost.
notes.math: The method treats deployment as a second learning stage: the signal supplies an unsupervised clue about the new domain while the enhancement objective remains the output target.
notes.ww: The paper reports consistent speech-quality improvements over its baseline on synthetic and real-world datasets.
notes.limits: The adaptation steps, compute budget, noise conditions, and author-reported metrics bound the result; listener benefit and long-term stability remain open.
notes.title: Test-Time Training for Speech Enhancement

notes.bp: A speech-based dementia score can correlate with human scores while still being systematically wrong for some people.
notes.wh: Word-naming performance and fallback rules can make severe impairment look easier to detect than mild impairment or healthy speech.
notes.naive: Report one overall correlation and treat it as equally meaningful across severity groups.
notes.ap: Inspect the automated Syndrom-Kurz-Test pipeline by subgroup, transcription quality, item type, and fallback behavior rather than relying on one aggregate number.
notes.mech: The analysis links scoring artifacts to speech production decline, ASR errors, and fallback handling; apparent agreement can therefore arise from the test design.
notes.math: The paper turns evaluation from a single correlation into a chain of measurement decisions whose errors can favor particular groups.
notes.ww: The paper reports high overall correlation but weaker behavior for healthy and mildly impaired groups and identifies overoptimistic correlations for severely impaired speakers.
notes.limits: This is an analysis of one standardized assessment and its data; it warns against clinical claims, not a universal ranking of dementia-screening systems.
notes.title: Pitfalls and Limits in Automatic Dementia Assessment

notes.bp: A text-to-speech system should pronounce an accent it has barely seen without requiring a large new pronunciation database.
notes.wh: Pronunciation frontend errors occur before waveform generation and are costly to label for every accent.
notes.naive: Train a separate full-size pronunciation model for every target accent.
notes.ap: Transfer pronunciation knowledge from a large multi-accent frontend and measure how much target-accent data is needed as source accents vary in similarity.
notes.mech: The frontend predicts phones, lexical stress, and prosodic boundaries; target accents are trained with reduced data and compared with full-data and single-accent baselines.
notes.math: Accent similarity becomes a data-selection variable: transfer is not merely shared representation, but choosing a source whose pronunciation structure is useful for the target.
notes.ww: The paper reports up to 95% less pronunciation training data for robust performance and examines 14 English accents using LibriTTS and HiFi-TTS-derived data.
notes.limits: Accuracy is reported for the studied accents, frontend labels, and datasets; transfer to other languages, voices, and synthesis backends remains unestablished.
notes.title: Non-Standard Accent TTS Support via Large Multi-Accent Frontend Pronunciation Knowledge Transfer

notes.bp: A recognizer must recognize rare or domain-specific words without paying the full cost of beam search on every utterance.
notes.wh: Greedy decoding is cheap but loses context; beam search recovers some context at a large compute cost.
notes.naive: Use beam search everywhere, or add a sequential language model whose data structure serializes every transition.
notes.ap: Represent n-gram transitions for parallel GPU lookup and inject their scores into greedy decoding for CTC, transducer, and attention models.
notes.mech: NGPU-LM uses hash-based transition lookup and customizable greedy decoding so context biasing can recover domain words with less than 7% reported overhead.
notes.math: The conceptual trade is between linguistic context and decoding latency; data structure and hardware choices move that boundary without changing the acoustic model.
notes.ww: The paper reports recovery of more than half the greedy/beam accuracy gap in out-of-domain tests and up to 10.6% relative WER improvement in its experiments.
notes.limits: The results depend on tested ASR architectures, domains, GPU implementation, and author-reported measurements; deployment energy and other hardware remain open.
notes.title: NGPU-LM: GPU-Accelerated N-Gram Language Model for Context-Biasing in Greedy ASR Decoding

notes.bp: A speech-quality score should remain meaningful when processing changes the timing of the speech, not only its spectrum.
notes.wh: Reference-based intelligibility predictors compare aligned clean and degraded signals; time modification breaks that alignment.
notes.naive: Use MFCC-based dynamic time warping or assume time modification is a small nuisance.
notes.ap: Align clean and time-modified speech with selected spectro-temporal modulation features, then feed the alignment into existing reference-based intelligibility predictors.
notes.mech: The system uses DTW over modulation features and compares two ways of incorporating the alignment into RB-SIPAs across noise and time-modification conditions.
notes.math: The move separates two questions that are often mixed: finding corresponding speech events and predicting whether the resulting signal is intelligible.
notes.ww: The paper reports better alignment behavior and better correlation with listening scores than MFCC-based alternatives under its tested conditions.
notes.limits: The listening datasets, degradation types, chosen modulation channels, and reference availability bound the claim; correlation is not a complete model of listener experience.
notes.title: Intelligibility Prediction for Time-Modified Speech Signals Using Spectro-Temporal Modulation Features

notes.bp: A recognizer needs to adapt to a new domain when only a little labeled speech is available but related audio is abundant.
notes.wh: Unlabeled audio can add coverage but can also inject wrong pseudo-labels and reinforce domain errors.
notes.naive: Fine-tune once on the small labeled set or choose pseudo-labels randomly.
notes.ap: Incrementally combine in-domain labels with related-domain data, then filter pseudo-labels using multi-model consensus or named-entity recognition.
notes.mech: The pipeline retrains in stages and uses agreement or entity preservation to decide which generated transcripts enter the next training round.
notes.math: Data selection is treated as part of learning: the value of unlabeled speech depends on which errors are admitted, not only on how much audio is added.
notes.ww: The paper reports up to 22.3% relative improvement on Wow and 24.8% on Fisher over random selection, with consensus strongest and NER cheaper.
notes.limits: The gains are bounded to the two English corpora, model ensemble, filtering thresholds, and author-reported WER; other domains and languages remain unresolved.
notes.title: Better Semi-supervised Learning for Multi-domain ASR Through Incremental Retraining and Data Filtering

notes.bp: Large child-speech collections need segment boundaries, but an adult-trained aligner may place those boundaries according to a different rule than a human analyst.
notes.wh: Children's articulation and developmental variation make forced alignment less stable, and disagreement can change measured vowel durations or trajectories.
notes.naive: Treat an adult forced aligner as interchangeable with manual annotation.
notes.ap: Compare human-human reliability with manual-versus-Montreal-Forced-Aligner boundaries across child ages and inspect systematic discrepancies.
notes.mech: The study evaluates vowel boundaries in Australian-English child speech and asks how alignment error changes from ages four to eleven.
notes.math: The conceptual issue is not simply alignment accuracy: a boundary is an analytic decision whose meaning must be shared by the tool and the human measurement protocol.
notes.ww: The paper reports that MFA falls short of human annotation, with smaller discrepancies for older children.
notes.limits: The evidence is tied to the tested vowels, ages, language variety, and annotators; it supports semi-automatic caution rather than universal aligner failure.
notes.title: ASR-based segmentation for the analysis of larger child-speech datasets: Performance evaluation on vowels from Australian-English speaking children aged 4 to 11 years

notes.bp: A spoof detector should recognize synthetic audio from new generators and public-domain conditions, not only the generator seen during training.
notes.wh: Semantic embeddings can learn the message instead of the traces of synthesis, while in-domain scores can hide failure under distribution shift.
notes.naive: Optimize only on a matched generator and report one in-domain score.
notes.ap: Use non-semantic universal audio representations and compare them with handcrafted, semantic, and end-to-end alternatives under out-of-domain tests.
notes.mech: TRILL and TRILLsson representations are evaluated as features for a spoofing classifier across in-domain and public-domain conditions.
notes.math: The method changes what evidence the detector is allowed to use: it seeks production artifacts that survive a change in spoken content and generator.
notes.ww: The paper reports comparable in-domain performance and stronger out-of-domain results than the tested baselines.
notes.limits: The generators, corpora, representation models, and author-reported tests define the boundary; future synthesis methods and adversarial adaptation remain open.
notes.title: Generalizable Audio Spoofing Detection using Non-Semantic Representations
